q: Which shell is the default on Snowball and most modern Linux systems?
explain: Bash is the most common modern shell; sh, ksh, and csh are its ancestors and cousins.

q: Which pair of protocols is encrypted?
explain: SSH encrypts a remote terminal session and SFTP runs file transfer over SSH. Telnet and FTP send everything in plaintext.

q: In an SFTP session, which command downloads a file from the server to your machine?
explain: get downloads, put uploads. Add -r for whole directories, and reget/reput to resume.

q: What does CTRL-Z do to a running process?
explain: CTRL-C kills, CTRL-Z suspends, CTRL-D sends end-of-file, CTRL-S pauses output.

q: A file is rw-r--r--. What does chmod g+w file produce?
explain: g+w adds write for the group only, leaving the owner and other triplets untouched.

q: Write the chmod command that adds execute for the owner and removes read for the group, and give the result for a file that starts as rw-r--r--.
answer: chmod u+x,g-r file. Starting from rw-r--r--, the owner gains x (rwx) and the group loses r (---), giving rwx---r--.
explain: Symbolic mode changes only the bits you name; octal mode would set all nine at once.

q: Which path is absolute?
explain: Absolute paths start at the root /. The others are relative to the current directory.

q: Which command counts the number of lines in a file?
explain: wc -l counts lines, -w counts words, -c counts bytes.

q: Who created C, and in what year did UNIX get rewritten in it?
explain: Dennis Ritchie extended Thompson's B into C by 1973, the same year UNIX was rewritten in C, which made it portable.

q: Which is NOT a property of C?
choices: Direct access to memory and system calls
explain: C has no OOP support. Structs group data, but there are no classes or inheritance.

q: Name the three stages of the C compilation pipeline and what each does.
answer: 1) Preprocessing: handles all # directives, expanding #include files, substituting #define macros, and stripping comments, producing pure C. 2) Compiling: translates the preprocessed source into machine instructions (object code, .o), catching syntax errors. 3) Linking: combines object files with library code into the final executable, a.out by default.
explain: Knowing the stage tells you where an error came from: a missing library is a link error, not a compile error.

q: Which gcc command compiles file.c into an executable named myprog?
explain: -o names the output. Plain gcc file.c produces a.out, and -lm links the math library.

q: Which basic type's size differs between 32-bit and 64-bit systems?
explain: long is 4 bytes on 32-bit and 8 on 64-bit. (Pointers also change size, but among the basic arithmetic types it is long.)

q: Uninitialized local variables in C are automatically set to zero.
explain: They contain whatever garbage was already in that memory. Always initialize.

q: After int a, b, c = 5; which variables are initialized?
choices: a and b to 0, c to 5
None; this is a syntax error
explain: The initializer applies only to the variable it follows. a and b hold garbage.

q: What does the integer literal 052 mean in C?
explain: A leading 0 means octal: 5×8 + 2 = 42. A leading 0x means hex.

q: Why does scanf need & for an int but not for a char array?
choices: An array name is already the address of its first element
explain: scanf must be told where to store the value. Scalars need &x; an array name already decays to a pointer.

q: Which specifier must you use with scanf to read a double?
explain: printf can use %f for a double, but scanf needs %lf to know the target is 8 bytes.

q: What does printf("%x", 255) print?
explain: %x prints lowercase hex with no 0x prefix; %X prints FF.

q: How many bytes does the string literal "Hello" occupy?
explain: Five characters plus the null terminator \0 = 6 bytes. strlen returns 5 because it does not count the terminator.

q: str1 = str2 copies one string into another in C.
explain: Assigning arrays is illegal in C. Use strcpy(str1, str2), and make sure the destination is large enough.

q: What does strcmp("Hello", "hello") return, and why?
explain: strcmp compares character by character; uppercase letters come before lowercase in ASCII, so the difference is negative.

q: What is wrong with char name[5]; strcpy(name, "Alexander"); and how do you fix it?
answer: "Alexander" is 9 characters plus the null terminator, so it needs 10 bytes, but name holds only 5. strcpy does no bounds checking, so it writes 5 bytes past the end of the array: a buffer overflow that can crash or corrupt memory. Fix by declaring a large enough buffer (char name[10];) or using strncpy and setting dst[n-1] = '\0' yourself.
explain: This is the single most-tested string pitfall.

q: Why does #define SQ(x) x*x give the wrong answer for SQ(2+3)?
choices: It expands to 2+3*2+3 = 11 because macros are plain text substitution
explain: Wrap each parameter and the whole body in parentheses: ((x)*(x)).

q: A static local variable inside a function:
choices: Keeps its value between calls but stays visible only inside that function
explain: static extends a local's lifetime to the whole program while leaving its scope unchanged.

q: What does extern int counter; do in file2.c?
choices: Allocates a new counter in file2.c
Declares that counter is defined in another file and links to it
explain: extern is a declaration, not a definition: no memory is allocated, and the linker connects it to the definition elsewhere.

q: Explain the dangling else problem using if (a) if (b) x = 1; else x = 2;
answer: The else binds to the nearest unmatched if, which is if (b), regardless of indentation. So x = 2 runs when a is true and b is false, not when a is false. Always use braces to make the pairing explicit.
explain: Indentation has no meaning to the C compiler.

q: What prints? int i = 0; switch(i) { case 0: printf("A"); case 1: printf("B"); break; default: printf("C"); }
explain: Case 0 matches and prints A, then falls through to case 1 and prints B, where break stops execution. Missing break causes fall-through.

q: Which loop is guaranteed to execute its body at least once?
explain: do-while tests the condition after the body, so the body always runs once. while and for test first and may run zero times.

q: What is the value of 5/2 in C, and how do you get 2.5?
explain: Two int operands give integer division, which truncates. Casting one operand to double forces floating-point division.

q: switch can test ranges of values and floating-point cases.
explain: switch compares against integer or character constants only. Use if-else for ranges or floats.

q: Why is if (x = 5) dangerous?
choices: It assigns 5 to x and is always true
explain: = assigns, == compares. The assignment's value is 5, which is non-zero, so the condition is always true. Defensive style: if (5 == x).

q: After int c[10] = {1, 2, 3}; what are elements 3 through 9?
explain: Partial initialization zeroes the remaining elements. Without any initializer, all elements hold garbage.

q: What does C do when you access a[5] in int a[5];?
choices: Nothing special: undefined behavior, possibly a crash or silent corruption
explain: C performs no bounds checking. Valid indices are 0 through 4.

q: Write a swap function that actually exchanges two ints in the caller, and explain why the obvious version fails.
answer: void swap(int *a, int *b) { int tmp = *a; *a = *b; *b = tmp; } called as swap(&x, &y). A version taking int a, int b fails because C passes by value: the function swaps its own copies and the caller's variables are unchanged.
explain: Passing the address is how C simulates pass-by-reference.

q: Inside int sum(int arr[], int n), what does sizeof(arr) return on a 64-bit machine?
choices: The total array size in bytes
explain: The array decayed to a pointer at the call, so sizeof gives the pointer size. Always pass the length separately.

q: Passing an array to a function copies the whole array.
explain: The array decays to a pointer to its first element, so the function works on the caller's actual data. This is the one case that behaves like pass-by-reference.

q: Every recursive function needs which two parts?
choices: A base case and a recursive case that shrinks the problem
A global variable and a return
explain: Without a base case the recursion never stops and the stack overflows.

q: In int *p = &x; *p = 50; what happens to x?
explain: p holds x's address, so dereferencing and assigning writes through to x.

q: Name four ways to create undefined behavior with pointers.
answer: 1) Using an uninitialized pointer, which holds a garbage address. 2) Dereferencing NULL, which causes a segmentation fault. 3) Using a dangling pointer to a local variable after its function returned. 4) Using a pointer to memory that has been freed (use-after-free). The rule is to always initialize pointers, setting them to NULL when there is nothing to point at yet.
explain: Use-after-free is a real vulnerability class, which your security course covers.

q: Which command records your terminal session to a file?
explain: script session.log captures everything until you exit, which is how lab evidence is usually submitted.

q: What does strcmp return when two strings are equal?
explain: 0 means equal, which is why the idiomatic equality test is !strcmp(s1, s2).

q: Which statement about static is correct?
choices: static on a local makes it visible to other functions
static on a global limits it to that source file
static means the variable cannot change
static is only valid on pointers
explain: static on a global restricts visibility to one file; static on a local extends lifetime while keeping scope.

q: Python has a do-while loop just like C.
explain: Python has no do-while. That construct is C and Java only, and the guide flags it as a trap.

q: What does return 0 from main() signal?
explain: 0 means success and non-zero signals an error, which is what shell scripts test.
